summary: Gives an architectural introduction to the Locator/ID Separation Protocol (LISP), to make the other LISP specifications easier to read and provide a basis for discussing their details. The protocol details are in RFC 9300 and RFC 9301. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Locating and identifying a computer are two different jobs, and the IP address does both at once. LISP gives each job its own kind of address: one that says what the computer is and one that says which router it hangs off. Routers in the middle of the Internet route on the second kind, which groups neatly, while the first kind stays with the computer when it moves.

subtitle: Splitting who a host is from where it is attached, so the Internet core can route on locators alone.

tldr.problem: An IP address says both who a node is and where it is attached, but routing needs addresses that aggregate by topology while nodes need identities that do not change when they move.
tldr.mechanism: LISP creates two namespaces: Endpoint Identifiers for hosts at the edge and Routing Locators for the core. Edge routers look up EID-to-RLOC mappings in a Mapping System and encapsulate packets towards the right RLOC.
tldr.outcome: The core routing system carries only aggregating locator addresses, so a host can move without changing anything in the core. This document is an introduction only; the protocol itself is in RFC 9300 and RFC 9301.

sections.title: Why Split Identity from Location
sections.content:
This document introduces the Locator/ID Separation Protocol architecture, its main operational mechanisms and its design rationale. LISP is built on a well-known architectural idea: decoupling the overloaded semantics of IP addresses. As Noel Chiappa pointed out, an IP address currently identifies both the topological location of a network attachment point and the node's identity, while nodes and routing have fundamentally different requirements. Routing systems require addresses that are aggregatable and have topological meaning; nodes must be identified independently of their current location.

LISP creates two separate namespaces, Endpoint Identifiers (EIDs) and Routing Locators (RLOCs). Both are syntactically identical to current IPv4 and IPv6 addresses. EIDs uniquely identify nodes irrespective of their topological location and are typically routed inside a domain. RLOCs are assigned topologically to network attachment points and are typically routed between domains. The edge of the Internet, where nodes are connected, and the core, where inter-domain routing happens, are logically separated. LISP-capable routers interconnect the two spaces, and a database called the Mapping System stores and retrieves the mappings between identity and location. LISP-capable routers exchange packets over the Internet core by encapsulating them towards the appropriate location.

The document summarises where each kind of address has meaning. RLOCs have meaning only in the underlay network, the underlying core routing system. EIDs have meaning only in the overlay network, the encapsulation relationship between LISP-capable routers. The LISP edge maps EIDs to RLOCs. Within the underlay network, RLOCs carry both locator and identifier semantics, while an EID inside a LISP site carries both identifier and locator semantics to other nodes in that site, and identifier with limited locator semantics to nodes at other sites, which is enough to tell that the EID is external to the site.

The initial motivation is the routing scalability problem. If LISP were completely deployed, the Internet core would be populated with RLOCs while traffic engineering mechanisms would be pushed into the Mapping System. RLOCs would then be quasi-static, with low churn, which makes the routing system scalable, while EIDs could roam anywhere with no churn to the underlying global routing system. The separation also makes LISP suitable for other scenarios: traffic engineering, multihoming, mobility, IPv6 coexistence, virtual private networks and virtual machine mobility in data centres.

The architecture rests on four design principles. The locator/identifier split lets devices have identity-based addresses separate from topologically meaningful ones, and only the latter reach the Internet core, where they can be aggregated. The overlay architecture routes packets over the current Internet, so new protocols can be deployed without changing the existing infrastructure and at low deployment cost. The decoupled data plane and control plane lets them scale independently and use different architectural approaches, which matters because they have different requirements, and also allows other data planes to be added; they are not completely isolated, because the data plane may trigger control plane activity. Incremental deployability ensures the protocol interoperates with the legacy Internet while giving early adopters some of the targeted benefits.
sections.plainLanguage: Two jobs are being split apart. Routing wants addresses that group by geography, so routers can summarise them. Hosts want an address that stays with them when they move. LISP keeps both and never mixes them up on the wire: the core only ever sees the geographic kind.

sections.title: The Pieces and How a Packet Travels
sections.content:
LISP splits the core from the edge of the Internet by creating the two namespaces. The edge consists of LISP sites, such as an Autonomous System, that use EID addresses; these are IPv4 or IPv6 addresses that uniquely identify communication end hosts and are assigned by the same mechanisms that exist today. EIDs carry no inter-domain topological information, so they are usually routable at the edge but not in the core.

LISP sites are connected to the core by LISP-capable routers, and LISP sites are connected to each other across the core using tunnels between those routers. Packets leaving a site enter an encapsulated tunnel at an Ingress Tunnel Router (ITR), and packets coming from the core leave an encapsulated tunnel at an Egress Tunnel Router (ETR). A router that can do both is called an xTR. With LISP the core uses RLOCs, which are IPv4 or IPv6 addresses assigned to a core-facing interface of an ITR or ETR.

A database, typically distributed and called the Mapping System, stores the mappings between EIDs and RLOCs. A mapping relates the identity of the devices attached to LISP sites to the set of RLOCs configured at the routers servicing the site, and can also carry traffic engineering policies and be configured to achieve multihoming and load balancing. The Mapping System is conceptually similar to the DNS, organised as a distributed multi-organization network database, with ETRs registering mappings and ITRs retrieving them.

The document then walks through a simplified packet flow, with client HostA sending to server HostB. HostA retrieves the EID of HostB, typically by querying the DNS for an A or AAAA record, and generates an ordinary IP packet with source EID_A and destination EID_B. The packet is forwarded to ITR_A inside the site using standard intra-domain mechanisms. ITR_A queries the Mapping System for the locator of the ETR servicing EID_B, using a Map-Request whose lookup key is EID_B, and receives a Map-Reply containing two locators, RLOC_B1 and RLOC_B2, along with traffic engineering policies giving a priority and a weight per locator; a Map-Reply can contain more locators if needed, and ITR_A can cache the mapping to speed up later packets.

ITR_A then encapsulates the packet towards RLOC_B1, chosen according to the priorities and weights in the mapping. The packet now has two IP headers: the outer header with RLOC_A1 as source and RLOC_B1 as destination, and the inner original header with EID_A and EID_B, plus a LISP header. The encapsulated packet is forwarded over the core as a normal IP packet, which keeps the EID invisible from the core. ETR_B decapsulates it and forwards the packet to HostB.
sections.plainLanguage: Each site has routers that speak LISP. When a packet leaves the site, the sending router asks a directory, the Mapping System, where the destination is actually connected. It then puts the original packet inside a new one addressed to that location, so the Internet in between carries only the outer address and never learns the inner one.

sections.title: The Four Headers of a LISP Packet
sections.content:
ITRs encapsulate data packets towards ETRs, and LISP data packets are encapsulated using UDP on port 4341. The source port is usually chosen by the ITR with a 5-tuple hash of the inner header, so that it stays consistent in multipath cases such as ECMP, and it is ignored on reception. LISP data packets are often encapsulated in UDP packets with a zero checksum that may not be verified on receipt, because the packet normally includes an inner transport header with a non-zero checksum; if the outer UDP checksum is non-zero it is verified as part of normal UDP processing.

A LISP-encapsulated packet also carries a LISP header, placed after the UDP header and before the original IP header. The LISP header is prepended by ITRs and stripped by ETRs, and carries reachability information and the Instance ID field, which distinguishes traffic to and from different tenant address spaces at the LISP site.

Overall LISP works on four headers, from outer to inner. The outer IP header contains the RLOCs as source and destination addresses; it is originated by ITRs and stripped by ETRs. The UDP header, on port 4341 and usually with a zero checksum, is originated by ITRs and stripped by ETRs. The LISP header carries forwarding-plane features such as reachability and the Instance ID; it is originated by ITRs and stripped by ETRs. The inner IP header contains the EIDs as source and destination addresses; it is created by the source end host and left unchanged by LISP processing on the ITR and the ETR.

ITRs keep only enough information to route traffic through them: the mappings between EID-Prefixes, blocks of EIDs, and the RLOCs used to encapsulate packets. Those mappings are stored in a local cache called the LISP Map-Cache. When EID-Prefixes overlap, a request can return a set of mappings covering the requested prefix and all more specific ones. Each mapping includes a Time to Live set by the ETR.

Finally, in some scenarios re-encapsulating and recursive tunnels are useful to choose a specified path in the underlay, for instance to avoid congestion or failure. Re-encapsulating tunnels are consecutive LISP tunnels, where a decapsulator removes a LISP header and then acts as an encapsulator to prepend another one. Recursive tunnels are nested tunnels, implemented with multiple LISP encapsulations on a packet. Both are implemented by Re-encapsulating Tunnel Routers, which first act as an ETR and then as an ITR.
sections.plainLanguage: A LISP packet has an outer address, a UDP header, a small LISP header and the original packet inside. The middle routers read only the outer address, and the receiving router strips the three added headers before handing the original packet on. The LISP header also carries an Instance ID that tells the receiver which tenant the packet belongs to.

sections.title: The Control Plane and the Mapping System
sections.content:
The LISP control plane provides a standard interface to register and request mappings, and the Mapping System is the database that stores them. Each mapping holds the bindings between one or more EID-Prefixes and a set of RLOCs, together with traffic engineering policies in the form of priorities and weights for the RLOCs. Priorities let the ETR configure active and backup policies, while weights are used to load-balance traffic among RLOCs on a per-flow basis. Typical mappings bind EIDs in the form of IP prefixes to a set of RLOCs; IPv4 and IPv6 addresses are encoded with the appropriate Address Family Identifier, and the LISP Canonical Address Format work allows more general address encodings that could support MAC addresses, geocoordinates, ASCII names and application-specific data.

The interface defines two entities. The Map-Server learns mappings from ETRs and publishes them into the Mapping System; typically it is not authoritative to reply to queries and forwards them to the ETR, though it can also operate in proxy mode where ETRs delegate replies to it, which is useful when the ETR has limited resources such as CPU or power. The Map-Resolver interfaces ITRs with the Mapping System by proxying queries and sometimes responses.

Four control messages are sent as UDP datagrams on port 4342. Map-Register is used by ETRs to register mappings in the Mapping System and is authenticated with a shared key between the ETR and the Map-Server. Map-Notify is sent by the Map-Server in response to a Map-Register, when requested, to acknowledge correct reception and convey the latest server state; in some cases it is sent to the previous RLOCs when an EID is registered by a new set of RLOCs. Map-Request is used by ITRs or Map-Resolvers to resolve the mapping of a given EID. Map-Reply is sent by Map-Servers or ETRs in response and contains the resolved mapping; it may contain a negative reply, for example when the queried EID is not part of the LISP EID space, in which case the ITR typically forwards the traffic as it is to the public Internet, which supports incremental deployment.

Several Mapping System designs have been explored: graph-based databases in the form of LISP-ALT, hierarchical databases in the form of LISP-DDT, monolithic databases in the form of LISP-NERD, flat databases in the form of a distributed hash table, and a multicast-based database. In private deployments the Mapping System can operate as logically centralized, typically a single Map-Server and Map-Resolver.

Of these, two have been implemented and deployed. LISP-ALT was the first, developed and deployed on the LISP pilot network; it is a distributed BGP overlay in which Map-Servers and Map-Resolvers participate, connected to their peers through static tunnels, and each Map-Server advertises the EID-Prefixes registered by the ETRs it serves, making the EID routable on the ALT topology. When an ITR needs a mapping it sends a Map-Request to a Map-Resolver, which forwards it over the ALT topology towards the responsible Map-Server, which forwards it to the ETR, which replies directly to the ITR. LISP-DDT is conceptually similar to the DNS: a hierarchical directory whose structure mirrors the EID address space, made of DDT nodes forming a tree whose leaves are Map-Servers, with a DDT root at the top matching the entire address space, redundant DDT nodes and roots, and Map-Resolvers as clients that can query the root or other nodes. The DDT structure does not index EID-Prefixes but Extended EID-Prefixes, which concatenate a Database-ID, an Instance ID, an Address Family Identifier and the EID-Prefix. Lookups work like DNS but only iteratively: a client sends a Map-Request to the DDT root and receives a Map-Referral, a further control message that lists the RLOCs of the DDT nodes matching the configured delegation, pointing at the child with more specific information. The process repeats until the client reaches the Map-Server servicing the queried prefix, then sends a Map-Request and receives a Map-Reply. Clients can cache the referrals, that is, the DDT structure, to speed up later lookups.

Because EIDs are usually not announced beyond the local LISP domain, LISP needs internetworking mechanisms. The Proxy Ingress Tunnel Router provides connectivity from the legacy Internet to LISP sites by announcing blocks of EID-Prefixes in the global routing system, aggregating where possible; for each incoming packet from a source that is not in a LISP site it LISP-encapsulates the packet towards the RLOCs of the appropriate site. The Proxy Egress Tunnel Router provides connectivity from LISP sites to the legacy Internet, which is needed when a site cannot send encapsulated packets with a local EID source address, for instance when Unicast Reverse Path Forwarding is used by Provider Edge routers or when an intermediate network does not support the desired IP version. LISP also defines LISP-NAT for operating with private EIDs, where the xTR replaces a private EID source address with a routable one.
sections.plainLanguage: The directory is itself a distributed system. Routers publish the mappings they are authoritative for, and a lookup can be answered directly or by walking a hierarchy like the DNS. Two implementations are described in detail, one built on BGP and one built as a tree, plus the proxy routers that let a LISP site talk to the rest of the Internet.

sections.title: Running LISP: Caches, Reachability, MTU and Mobility
sections.content:
Because mappings live in the control plane and are used for forwarding in the data plane, ITRs need a local cache to reduce signalling overhead and increase forwarding speed. The Map-Cache is indexed by Instance ID and EID-Prefix and holds the set of RLOCs with their priorities and weights. Three mechanisms keep it coherent. A record Time to Live is set by the ETR on each mapping record; once it expires the ITR cannot use the mapping until it refreshes it with a new Map-Request. A Solicit-Map-Request is an explicit mechanism in which an ETR asks ITRs on demand to refresh their mappings, and the ITR must respond by sending a Map-Request to the Mapping System. Map-Versioning is an optional mechanism that piggybacks the version number of the mappings used by an xTR in the LISP header of data packets, so that a receiving xTR can tell whether its own cache or the remote xTR's cache is outdated, and refresh or send an SMR as appropriate.

In a pull-based Mapping System the network state sits in the control plane and the data plane pulls it on demand, so reachability and liveness information has to be propagated explicitly. Locator-Status-Bits are a passive technique: the LSB field in the LISP header of data packets can be set by ETRs to say which of their RLOCs are up or down, which ITRs use as a hint. They do not give path reachability, only hints about RLOC status, so they must not be used over the public Internet and should be paired with Map-Versioning. The Echo-Nonce technique works when traffic flows bidirectionally between two xTRs: the ITR piggybacks a random number in LISP data packets, and if the path and the probed locator are up the ETR piggybacks the same number back on the next data packet, otherwise the ITR can mark the locator unreachable; it must be used in trusted environments only. RLOC-Probing is active: the ITR sends probes to specific locators, effectively probing both the locator and the path, by sending a Map-Request with certain flags on the data plane and waiting for a Map-Reply sent on the data plane. Being active, it determines reachability and lets the ITR switch to a different locator, and it also gives round-trip time estimates useful to other algorithms. RLOC-Probing and Echo-Nonce work together: if a nonce is not echoed the ITR cannot tell which path direction failed, and can then probe. LISP also recommends inferring locator reachability from the underlay, from ICMP Network Unreachable or Host Unreachable messages, and from BGP or IGP reachability information.

All ETRs authoritative for a particular EID-Prefix must announce the same mapping, which means they must be aware of the status of each other's RLOCs. This is ETR synchronization, and at the time of writing LISP does not specify a mechanism for it, so operators must rely on coherent manual configuration.

Because LISP encapsulates packets, packets can exceed the MTU of the path between the ITR and the ETR. The stateless mechanism assumes the effective MTU from the ITR's perspective, and if a payload packet is too big and can be fragmented, the ITR fragments it so that reassembly happens at the destination host. The stateful mechanism has ITRs track the MTU of paths towards the destination locators by parsing ICMP Too Big packets from intermediate routers, sending ICMP Too Big messages to inform the sources, and using Path MTU Discovery or Packetization Layer Path MTU Discovery to keep track of the MTU towards the locators. In both cases, if the packet cannot be fragmented, because IPv4 has DF set or it is IPv6, the ITR drops it and replies with an ICMP Too Big message to the source.

Separating locators from identifiers is what makes mobility possible. A LISP site can change its attachment points, and its RLOCs, without affecting endpoints or the Internet core, with the border routers operating the xTR functionality and endpoints unaware of LISP; this is similar to Network Mobility. That mode does not allow seamless mobility of endpoints between different LISP sites, because the EID address might not be routable in a visited site, but LISP can enable seamless IP mobility when it is implemented directly in the endpoint or when the endpoint roams to an attached xTR. Each endpoint is then an xTR: the EID is the address presented to the network stack used by applications, and the RLOC is the address gathered from the network where it is visited, which is similar to Mobile IP. Whenever a device changes its RLOC, the xTR updates the RLOC of its local mapping and registers it to its Map-Server, typically with a low TTL value of 1 min, and also indicates the RLOC change to all remote devices with which it has ongoing communications, so that no home gateway is needed and signalling stays limited to the Map-Server and to those peers. LISP also supports IP multicast packets sent from the EID space: multicast state can be created at the core and at the sites, PIM Join and Prune messages from receivers to source sites are encapsulated as unicast packets, and at the core ETRs build a new PIM Join and Prune addressed to the RLOC of the ITR servicing the source.
sections.plainLanguage: Running the system comes down to three practical problems. The cached directory entries have to be kept fresh, so there is an expiry time, an explicit refresh request and a version number in the packet header. The router has to know whether the far end is still there, which it can check passively in the data packets, with an echo, or by probing. And because the packet is wrapped, it may become too big for the path, so there is a choice between guessing the size and tracking it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
In a push Mapping System the state needed to forward packets is learned independently of the traffic, but with a pull architecture the system becomes reactive, and data plane events such as the arrival of a packet with an unknown destination address may trigger control plane events. That on-demand learning has advantages but affects how security is enforced.

The data plane is normally implemented in the fast path of routers while the control plane sits in the slow path, and the two can differ in performance by several orders of magnitude. The way the control plane is notified of data plane events must therefore be considered carefully so as not to overload the slow path, and rate limiting should be used as specified in the LISP specifications. Care must also be taken not to overload the Mapping System itself, since the operations there may be more complex than those on the data plane, so rate limiting of messages to the Mapping System is recommended.

To improve resiliency and reduce the number of messages exchanged, LISP makes it possible to leak certain information, such as the reachability of locators, directly into data plane packets. In environments that are not fully trusted, like the open Internet, control information gleaned from data plane packets must not be used, or must be verified before use.

Mappings are the centrepiece of LISP, and all precautions must be taken to prevent malicious entities from manipulating or misusing them. Using trustworthy Map-Servers that strictly respect the LISP specifications, together with the authentication mechanism proposed by LISP-SEC, reduces the risk of attacks on mapping integrity; in more critical environments further measures may be needed. How security is implemented for a given Mapping System depends on the architecture of that Mapping System and the threat model assumed for the deployment, so Mapping System security has to be discussed in the documents proposing that architecture.

As with any other tunnelling mechanism, middleboxes on the path between an ITR and an ETR must implement mechanisms to strip the LISP encapsulation in order to inspect the content of LISP-encapsulated packets correctly. Like other map-and-encap mechanisms, LISP enables triangular routing, where the packets of a flow cross different border routers depending on their direction, which means intermediate boxes may have an incomplete view of the traffic they inspect or manipulate. LISP-encapsulated packets are routed on the outer IP address and can be delivered to an ETR that is not responsible for the destination EID, or even to a network element that is not an ETR at all; the mitigation is to apply appropriate filtering on the network elements that might receive such packets unexpectedly.
sections.plainLanguage: Two risks stand out. A packet with an unknown destination makes the router ask the directory, so an attacker can make the control plane work, and the rate limiting that stops that is important. And because the real destination is hidden inside the packet, a device in the middle cannot see what is really being carried unless it knows how to unwrap it.

layers.label: Outer IP header
layers.detail: RLOCs as source and destination. Originated by the ITR, stripped by the ETR.

layers.label: UDP header
layers.detail: Port 4341, usually with a zero checksum. Originated by the ITR, stripped by the ETR.

layers.label: LISP header
layers.detail: Reachability information and the Instance ID that separates tenant address spaces. Originated by the ITR, stripped by the ETR.

layers.label: Inner IP header
layers.detail: EIDs as source and destination. Created by the source host and left unchanged by LISP.

viz.caption: THE PACKET FLOW BETWEEN TWO LISP SITES

messages.label: Map-Reply
messages.note: RLOC_B1 and RLOC_B2, with a priority and a weight per locator.

messages.label: Encapsulated packet
messages.note: Outer header from RLOC_A1 to RLOC_B1; the EIDs stay invisible in the core.

viz.caption: THE LISP CONTROL MESSAGES, SENT ON UDP PORT 4342

items.label: ETR to Map-Server
items.desc: Registers an EID-to-RLOC mapping, authenticated with a shared key between the ETR and the Map-Server.

items.label: Map-Server to ETR
items.desc: Acknowledges correct reception of a mapping and conveys the latest Map-Server state.

items.label: ITR or Map-Resolver to Mapping System
items.desc: Asks for the mapping of a given EID.

items.label: Map-Server or ETR to ITR
items.desc: Carries the resolved mapping, or a negative reply when the EID is not part of the LISP EID space.

items.label: DDT node to Map-Resolver
items.desc: Introduced by LISP-DDT, it lists the RLOCs of the DDT nodes matching a delegation, pointing at the child with more specific information.
